meta.ogDescription: Attributed, not verified: one eyewitness, Bart Starr, and a wording that reaches print decades after Lombardi's 1959 Green Bay Packers team meeting.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely and credibly credited to Lombardi’s first team meeting as Packers head coach in 1959, on the word of one eyewitness — quarterback Bart Starr. But nothing recorded in 1959 preserves it: the wording reaches print through Starr’s recollection in two books published in 2004, and the closing sentence circulates in more than one form.

source.excerpt: Gentlemen, we are going to relentlessly chase perfection, knowing full well we will not catch it, because nothing is perfect. But we are going to relentlessly chase it, because in the process we will catch excellence. I am not remotely interested in just being good.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ carries this exact wording, dates it to Lombardi’s first team meeting as Packers coach in 1959, and cites Chuck Carlson, Game of My Life: 25 Stories of Packers Football (2004), p. 149 and Richard Scott & Jay Barker, Legends of Alabama Football (2004), p. 78.

Both of those citations run through one witness. Packer Report’s Tom Andrews recorded Bart Starr’s telling of the speech ↗, including the aside that Lombardi emphasised the word relentlessly — and a closing sentence worded differently from the one that circulates.
Lombardi’s official family site ↗ publishes only the compressed form, “Perfection is not attainable. But if we chase perfection, we can catch excellence.” — not the “Gentlemen” speech.
Quote Investigator’s Lombardi archive ↗ holds three investigations and none of them is this saying, so there is no specialist ruling to defer to — which is why this page stops at attributed.
source.excerptNote: That is the wording in Wikiquote’s sourced section. Starr’s own telling, as recorded by Packer Report, runs slightly differently: “… knowing full well we will not catch it. Nothing is perfect but we are going to relentlessly — and he emphasized relentlessly — chase it because, in the process, we will catch excellence,” closing “I am not even remotely interested in being just good.”

author.name: Vince Lombardi
author.kicker: The man it is credited to
author.heading: Who was Vince Lombardi?
author.metaLine: 1913–1970 · NFL head coach · Pro Football Hall of Fame, Class of 1971
author.bio: Born in Brooklyn on 11 June 1913, Lombardi was hired as head coach of the Green Bay Packers on 2 February 1959 and turned a losing franchise into the defining dynasty of 1960s professional football, going 9–1 in post-season play with an overall coaching record of 105–35–6. He left Green Bay after the 1967 season, stayed on as general manager in 1968, and returned to the sideline with Washington in 1969 before cancer killed him on 3 September 1970. He was elected to the Pro Football Hall of Fame with the Class of 1971, and his name is now attached to more motivational sayings than he can be shown to have originated.

misattribution.heading: What gets mangled
misattribution.intro: This one is not a fake — but almost nobody quotes it the way the sourced record has it, and Lombardi’s name attracts sayings that were never his.

items.why: The version in near-universal circulation — “Perfection is not attainable, but if we chase perfection we can catch excellence” — is a boiled-down form, not the remembered speech. Lombardi’s own family site ↗ publishes only that short version, without the “Gentlemen” opening or the closing sentence.

Wikiquote’s sourced entry ends “I am not remotely interested in just being good.” Packer Report’s Tom Andrews recorded Starr telling it as “I am not even remotely interested in being just good” — and noted that Lombardi emphasised the word relentlessly ↗.

Lombardi is one of the internet’s great quote magnets. Quote Investigator ascribes his most famous line, “Winning isn’t everything; it’s the only thing,” to Henry ‘Red’ Sanders in 1948 ↗ — so a Lombardi attribution deserves checking by default.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the occasion are almost certainly genuine — a named Hall of Fame eyewitness told this story consistently — but the words we quote are Bart Starr’s memory, reaching print in the 2004 books Wikiquote cites ↗, not a 1959 transcript.

context.heading: Why a locker-room line became a management slogan
lead: Lombardi took over the Green Bay Packers on 2 February 1959, at forty-five, inheriting a franchise that had become a punchline. The line Bart Starr remembered from that first meeting is not a maxim about winning — it is a maxim about the gap between the target you aim at and the result you can actually hold. Chase something unreachable, Lombardi is said to have told the room, and what you end up holding is excellence.

That structure is exactly why the sentence escaped football. Stripped to its compressed form — the version Lombardi’s own family site publishes — it became one of the most reproduced sayings in corporate training decks, sports halls and classroom posters. The compression is also what makes it hard to verify: what circulates is not a transcript but a remembered speech, boiled down over decades of retelling.
detailsBody: A 1959 team meeting was a closed room. There were no cameras, no stenographer and no reason for a reporter to be present — so the absence of a contemporaneous record is not itself suspicious. What it does mean is that every published version of these words descends from recollection, and recollection drifts.

The drift is visible. Wikiquote’s sourced entry ends “I am not remotely interested in just being good.” Packer Report’s account of Starr telling the story ends “I am not even remotely interested in being just good,” and adds a stage direction — that Lombardi leaned on the word relentlessly. Neither is wrong; neither is a transcript.
context.pull: Perfection is not attainable. But if we chase perfection, we can catch excellence.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced Quotes section carries the exact wording "Gentlemen, we are going to relentlessly chase perfection ... I am not remotely interested in just being good." and cites it to Lombardi's first team meeting as Packers coach (1959), reported in Chuck Carlson, Game of My Life: 25 Stories of Packers Football (2004), p. 149, and Richard Scott, Jay Barker, Legends of Alabama Football (2004), p. 78.
Quote Investigator's Vince Lombardi category lists three articles and contains no investigation of the "chase perfection / catch excellence" saying.
Quote Investigator ascribes "Winning isn't everything; it's the only thing" to Henry 'Red' Sanders, who made the remark on 9 November 1948, and notes Lombardi later preferred a different formulation.

The official Vince Lombardi family site publishes the compressed form "Perfection is not attainable. But if we chase perfection, we can catch excellence." and its footer reads "© 2026 Family of Vince Lombardi c/o Luminary Group LLC", with licensing directed to Luminary Group.

Packer Report's Tom Andrews records Bart Starr's telling of Lombardi's speech as "...knowing full well we will not catch it. Nothing is perfect but we are going to relentlessly – and he emphasized relentlessly – chase it because, in the process, we will catch excellence," closing "I am not even remotely interested in being just good."

Richard Gunderman (Indiana University), writing in The Conversation on 16 December 2019, quotes the long form verbatim, attributes it to Lombardi's first meeting with the Packers team, and credits Game of My Life: Green Bay Packers (Skyhorse Publishing).

The Pro Football Hall of Fame records that Lombardi began coaching the Packers in 1959 at age 45, went 105-35-6 overall with a .740 winning percentage and 9-1 in post-season play, and was inducted with the Class of 1971.

Wikipedia gives Vince Lombardi's birth date as 11 June 1913 in Brooklyn, New York, his death as 3 September 1970, and records that he was hired as Green Bay Packers head coach on 2 February 1959, serving as head coach 1959-1967 and continuing as general manager in 1968.
Packers.com's Bart Starr Hall of Fame page confirms Starr's Packers career ran 1956-71 and that Lombardi took over as coach in 1959.
Sports Publishing / Skyhorse lists Game of My Life Green Bay Packers by Chuck Carlson and Bob Harlan, published 1 September 2012, described as a newly revised edition of Carlson's book.
